newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electric futures settle higher in late jump.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electric futures settle higher in late jump.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled higher Friday, erasing early losses tied to lackluster heating demand in the West and falling natural gas futures.
"It's just short-covering," said an East Coast electricity broker, characterizing to the day's late surge.
February California-Oregon Border (COB) futures settled up 59 cents at $14.23 a megawatt hour (MWh), near the day's high of $14.25. The contract hit a low of $13.40.
March COB ended up 26 cents at $11.91. The summer 1997 COB contracts finished 15-25 cents lower.
February Palo Verde (PV) settled up 43 cents at $16.08, erasing a 10 cent loss. March PV ended up 15 cents at $13.95. Most deferred PV contracts were inactive.
In over-the-counter activity after settlement, February COB was quoted at $13.90-$14.50 and February PV $15.85-$16.20.
In other forward business, February electricity deliveries in the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnect pool finished the day at $28.70-$28.85, lower than Wednesday's $28.90-$29.60.
Forecasts showed the Northwest would experience slightly below-normal temperatures through the weekend with chances of coastal rain and mountain snow.
Meanwhile, the Southwest would enjoy a warming trend through the weekend with above-normal precipitation for California and the Great Basin with below normal precipitation in the desert Southwest.
"I can't see it'll carry over. Gas didn't even go up today," replied another paper broker, when asked about the prospect of the electricity complex for Friday.
NYMEX February Henry Hub gas futures settled down 11.4 cents at $2.795 per million British thermal units.
February gas deliveries to the San Juan/Blanco Hub were assessed near $2.30-$2.35, down from Wednesday's $2.55.
Separately, a 750 megawatt (MW) power turbine at the Grand Coulee hydroelectric dam in Washington state remained off line after being shut for unplanned repairs Tuesday.
The refueling outage of the 1,070 MW unit 2 at the San Onofre nuclear power plant could into mid-February.
A 500 kilvolt transmission line, which runs from Snohomish County, Wash. to the Canadian border, could stay down until next week after damage from an ice storm late last week.

The outage of the 350 megawatt (MW) unit 1 at the Comanche coal-fired power plant in Pueblo, Colorado, was extended to approximately January 29 as more time was needed to repair damages from a fire in mid-December.
NYMEX estimated 318 COB and 112 PV contracts were sold.
